title: Saving in the browser
lesson:
Close the tab and your to-do list is gone: every variable lives only while the page is open. For a small offline app you don't need a server to remember things. The browser gives every site a little notebook called **localStorage**.

```
localStorage.setItem("water.buckets", "12");   // save
localStorage.getItem("water.buckets");         // "12" (or null if never saved)
localStorage.removeItem("water.buckets");      // forget
```

It survives closing the tab, closing the browser and restarting the computer. Two facts shape everything else:
- It stores **text only**. Save an array directly and you get the useless text `"[object Object]"`.
- `getItem` gives **null** for a key that was never saved.

**JSON turns data into text and back.**

```
localStorage.setItem("farm.todos", JSON.stringify(todos));    // array to text
const todos = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("farm.todos")); // text to array
```

**Load on start, save on every change.** The pattern for an app with state: when the page opens, load the state (or a sensible default); every time the state changes, save it. A good place is right next to `render()`: change state, save, render.

**Expect broken data.** Saved data can be missing (first visit, or the person cleared their browser), broken (an old version of your app saved a different shape, or someone edited it by hand), or simply not what you expect. `JSON.parse` *throws* on broken text and would stop your whole app on load, leaving a blank page. So loading is defensive:

```
function loadTodos() {
  try {
    const data = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("farm.todos"));
    return Array.isArray(data) ? data : [];
  } catch (err) {
    return [];          // broken text: start fresh instead of crashing
  }
}
```

`JSON.parse(null)` gives `null`, which isn't an array, so a missing key also falls back to `[]`. For important data you can go further: keep only items that look right (`typeof item.name === "string"`).

**Good habits.**
- Name keys with your app in them (`"chama.payments"`), so two apps on the same site don't overwrite each other. Adding a version (`"chama.v1"`) helps when the shape changes later.
- Return a *copy* of defaults (`{ ...DEFAULTS }`), not the defaults object itself, so changing settings can't change the defaults.
- Know the limits: about 5 MB per site, only on this browser on this computer, and visible to anyone using it. Fine for a game's high score or a group's records on a shared clinic laptop; not a place for passwords. Games use exactly this for save slots and settings.

notes: One key, named after the app, with a version.
JSON.stringify before saving, because localStorage holds only text.
try/catch around JSON.parse: a broken save starts a new game instead of crashing.
{ ...NEW_GAME, ...data } fills in fields an older save didn't have, and returns a fresh copy.

exercises.title: Save and load settings
exercises.prompt: Keep var DEFAULTS = { theme: "light", fontSize: 16 }. Write saveSettings(settings), which stores the object as JSON under the key "archie.settings". Write loadSettings(), which returns the saved settings on top of the defaults (a saved { theme: "dark" } gives { theme: "dark", fontSize: 16 }). If nothing is saved, or the saved text is broken, return a COPY of DEFAULTS.

exercises.title: Broken data doesn't crash
exercises.prompt: The clinic's stock is an array like [{ name: "ORS", qty: 30 }] saved under the key "clinic.stock". The starter has two classic bugs. Fix saveStock(stock) so it saves JSON. Fix loadStock() so it never crashes: it returns [] if nothing is saved, if the text is broken, or if the saved value isn't an array; and it keeps only items that are objects with a text name and a number qty (anything else is dropped).

quiz.why: localStorage holds text only; use JSON.stringify first.

quiz.q: Why wrap JSON.parse of saved data in try/catch?
choices: Broken saved text makes it throw, which would stop the app on load
quiz.why: Fall back to a fresh start instead of a blank page.

quiz.q: When should an app save its state?
quiz.why: Saving on each change means nothing is lost if the tab closes or crashes.

quiz.q: Which is a poor use of localStorage?
quiz.why: Anyone using that browser can read it; it isn't for secrets.

explain: Explain how you'd make an app remember its data between visits, and what could go wrong when loading it, with a made-up app.
